title: Brand Expansion & Distribution
subtitle: Take your product beyond direct sales into shops, distributors, marketplaces and agent networks, while protecting your brand and knowing the true profit of every channel.
description: An advanced, hands-on course for producers who already sell steadily and want to reach buyers they cannot reach alone. You will check your readiness, set brand and price rules, write partner agreements, build order-to-cash and quality routines, calculate true margin per channel, pitch retailers, manage agents and plan one new channel over 90 days.
outcomes: Measure the revenue share, profit share and risk of each of your sales channels
Score your readiness and choose a first new channel that fits your product, capacity and cash
Set brand standards, an RRP and a floor price, and write a one-page supply agreement
Run order-to-cash, batch coding and shelf-check routines across partners
Calculate the margin waterfall and true profit per unit and per month for each channel
Pitch retailers, run trial orders, manage agents and write a 90-day expansion plan
audience: Women producers and traders in Nigeria and across Africa who already sell a consistent product directly and want to grow through retail, wholesale, online and agent channels.
tools: Google Sheets or a notebook for logs and calculations
Canva or Google Docs for a sell sheet
Your sales records for the last one to three months
Product samples and your current label

modules.title: Channels, Readiness and Brand Rules
modules.overview: You start by measuring where your sales really come from, then test whether your product, packaging, capacity, cash and prices are ready for a new channel. You finish the module with written brand standards and the terms every distribution agreement should cover.

lessons.title: Mapping your sales channels and how concentrated they are
objectives: Name the main distribution channels open to a Nigerian small producer and how each one pays you
Explain how each layer between you and the buyer takes a share of the shelf price
Calculate the revenue share of each of your current channels
Judge how exposed your business is when one channel carries most of your income

blocks.text: Most small producers grow by selling directly: WhatsApp orders, Instagram DMs, a market stall, friends at church or work. Direct selling gives you the full price and close contact with buyers, but it has a ceiling. You can only sell to the people who already find you, and every sale needs your time. **Distribution** means building routes to buyers you would never reach alone, through businesses and people who already have those buyers' trust and attention.

This course is for producers who already sell steadily and now want to go further: into shops, supermarkets, pharmacies, online marketplaces, distributors and agent networks. It assumes you already have a product, a label and a cost price. Here you learn how to choose channels, protect your brand when other people sell it, and check that each channel truly makes money.

blocks.name: business-shop
blocks.alt: A small shop front with products on display
blocks.caption: A shop that stocks your product is a channel: it brings its own customers to your brand.

blocks.text: The main channels and how each one pays you

head: Channel
How it works
How you get paid
rows: Direct
You sell to the final customer: WhatsApp, Instagram, stall, your own payment link
Full price, usually paid before or on delivery
Retail, outright purchase
A shop buys stock from you and resells it
Trade price, paid on delivery or after agreed credit days
Retail, consignment
A shop displays your stock but pays only for what sells
Trade price for sold units, after a stock count
Distributor or wholesaler
Buys in bulk and supplies many shops in an area
A lower price than the shop pays, often on credit
Agents or resellers
Individuals sell for you in their own networks
Commission per sale, or a reseller discount
Online marketplace
A platform such as Jumia or Konga lists your product to its shoppers
Sale price minus the platform's fees, paid out on the platform's schedule

blocks.text: Notice two things in the table. First, every channel except direct selling gives part of the shelf price to someone else. That is fair: they bring the customers, the shelf space and often the delivery. Second, many channels pay you **later**. A shop that pays after 30 days is lending money to itself from your pocket. Both facts change your profit and your cash, and you will calculate them carefully in Module 2.

blocks.title: A long route to market
items: You, the maker
Distributor
Retail shop
Final customer
blocks.caption: Each step between you and the customer keeps part of the shelf price, so longer routes reach more people but leave you a smaller share per unit.

blocks.text: Channel concentration: how exposed are you?

Before adding anything new, measure what you have. **Channel concentration** is how much of your revenue depends on one channel. If one channel brings most of your money, a single disruption (your Instagram account is hacked, the market is closed for repairs, a salon owner relocates) cuts most of your income overnight. Spreading sales across two or three healthy channels makes the business steadier.

blocks.title: Worked example: measuring channel share
blocks.context: For example, Amaka makes whipped shea body butter in 250 g jars in Abuja. Her direct price is about 4,000 naira (approximate). Last month she sold 400 jars.
steps: WhatsApp and Instagram orders: 260 jars x 4,000 = 1,040,000 naira.
Saturday market stall: 100 jars x 4,000 = 400,000 naira.
One salon that buys from her at 2,800 naira a jar: 40 jars x 2,800 = 112,000 naira.
blocks.result: Two thirds of Amaka's income depends on her phone and social media accounts. Her expansion goal is not just more sales but a better spread, so that no single channel can sink the month.

blocks.text: Notice that the salon brings only 7.2% of revenue but 10% of the jars (40 of 400). Units and naira tell different stories because the salon pays a lower price. Always look at both, and later you will add a third view: profit per channel.

blocks.title: Use real records, not memory
blocks.text: Take the figures from your sales book, WhatsApp order list or bank and POS statements for the last one to three months. Memory usually overestimates the channel you enjoy most and forgets small, regular buyers.
Three shifts that come with distribution

items: **From one channel to several working together.** Your social media can send buyers to the shops that stock you, and shop presence makes your online brand look established.
**From a personal brand to a product brand.** Today many customers buy because they know you. On a supermarket shelf your jar must sell itself through its name, label, price and quality.
**From selling every unit to enabling others to sell.** Your job moves towards supplying, training, invoicing and checking, rather than chatting to every buyer.

blocks.text: None of these shifts happens by accident. A producer who rushes into five shops at once often runs out of stock, chases unpaid invoices and lets quality slip, and the brand suffers. The rest of this course gives you a careful order: measure, check readiness, set your rules, build simple systems, run the numbers, then pitch and grow one channel at a time.

blocks.title: Words you will meet
blocks.text: Trade price: what a shop pays you. Recommended retail price (RRP): the shelf price you advise. Margin: the share of a selling price that someone keeps as gross profit. Sell-through: the share of delivered stock that actually sells in a period.

takeaways: Every channel beyond direct selling keeps part of the shelf price, and many pay you later.
Measure each channel's share of revenue and of units before adding a new one.
If one channel carries most of your income, one disruption can sink the month.
Distribution moves you from selling every unit to supplying and supporting others who sell.

activity.title: Build your channel baseline
steps: List every way you sold last month, including friends, family and occasional bulk buyers.
For each channel, write units sold and the price each buyer paid.
Calculate revenue per channel and each channel's percentage of total revenue.
Mark your biggest channel and write one sentence on what would happen if it stopped for a month.
Note which channel types from the table you have never tried.
activity.evidence: A one-page channel baseline table (paper photo or Google Sheet) with units, revenue and percentage share for each channel.

lessons.title: Readiness check: product, capacity, cash and choosing your first new channel
objectives: Score your business on a five-part distribution readiness check
Calculate whether your production capacity can carry a new channel's orders
Estimate the cash a credit-based channel will tie up
Choose a first new channel that fits your product and readiness

blocks.text: A new shop relationship rarely fails because the owner is unkind. It fails because the supplier was not ready: the jars arrived with a different label from the sample, the second order came three weeks late, or the producer ran out of cash while waiting to be paid. This lesson gives you a readiness check to complete **before** you pitch anyone.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: Score yourself honestly on each readiness area before you approach a new partner.

blocks.text: The five-part readiness check
Score each area 0 (not ready), 1 (partly ready) or 2 (ready). A total of 8 to 10 means you can pitch. Below 8, fix the weakest area first.

head: Area
Ready (score 2) looks like
rows: 1. Product consistency
Every batch looks, smells and performs the same; you have a written recipe or method and a batch record
2. Packaging and paperwork
A finished label with all required information; CAC registration; NAFDAC registration where your product type needs it; a barcode if supermarkets are the target
3. Capacity
You can make the extra units every month without starving your existing customers
4. Pricing headroom
Your trade price covers your cost with profit left after the partner's margin
5. Cash and admin
You can fund stock while you wait to be paid, and you can issue invoices and keep an order log

blocks.text: On paperwork: formal retailers, supermarkets and pharmacies usually ask whether a food, drink, cosmetic or similar regulated product carries a NAFDAC registration number, and many will not list it without one. Supermarket tills scan barcodes, and in Nigeria barcodes are issued through GS1 Nigeria. Ask each target retailer for their exact supplier requirements rather than guessing; the list varies from shop to shop.
Capacity: do the maths before you say yes

blocks.title: Worked example: can she supply a pharmacy chain?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka (from the last lesson) makes about 400 jars a month and can stretch to 500 with her current kitchen, equipment and two helpers. A pharmacy chain with 4 branches asks for 24 jars per branch every two weeks.
steps: Monthly demand from the chain: 4 branches x 24 jars x 2 deliveries = 192 jars.
New total demand: 400 existing + 192 = 592 jars a month.
Gap: 592 - 500 maximum = 92 jars short every month.

Cash tied up: if each jar costs her about 1,900 naira (approximate) to make and the chain pays 30 days after delivery, she must fund at least 192 x 1,900 = 364,800 naira of stock before the first payment arrives.
Options: start with 2 branches (96 jars a month, total 496, within capacity), add a production day, or delay until she has the cash.
blocks.result: Amaka agrees to start with 2 branches. She stays within capacity, needs about 182,400 naira (96 x 1,900) of working cash instead of 364,800, and can add branches once the first two prove the product sells.

blocks.title: Never starve your loyal buyers
blocks.text: If a new channel takes stock your direct customers were waiting for, you trade a known, full-price customer for an unproven, lower-price one. Protect existing demand first, then add.
Matching the channel to your product

Different channels suit different products. Ask four questions: Does the product sell on sight, or does it need explaining? Is it fragile, heavy or perishable? How long is its shelf life? Is the price high enough to carry another party's margin?

items: **Shops and supermarkets** suit products that sell on sight, have a good shelf life and look strong next to competing brands.
**Online marketplaces** suit products that photograph well, survive courier delivery and have a clear size or variant.
**Agents and resellers** suit products that benefit from a personal recommendation, a demonstration or local trust.
**Distributors** suit products with steady demand across many shops, where you can afford a further margin layer.

blocks.title: Choosing your first new channel
items: Start here
Plan and build up
Small test only
Avoid for now
axes: Effort and cost to enter: low to high
Fit with your product: low to high
blocks.caption: Place each possible channel by how well it fits your product and how much work it takes to enter, then start in the top-left box.

blocks.text: For Amaka, a few nearby pharmacies and salons fit well and need little new investment, so they sit top-left. A national supermarket chain fits the product but needs a barcode, larger volumes and long credit, so it sits top-right: a goal for later. A marketplace would mean shipping heavy glass jars across the country, so she treats it as a small test only.
Write a one-line channel decision

Finish with a short statement: which channel first, why it fits, what must change before you pitch, and how you will judge it. For example: "I will supply 2 pharmacy branches in Wuse and Garki because my product sells on sight and they are 20 minutes away. Before pitching I will add batch codes and print a price list. I will judge it after 8 weeks on sell-through, on-time payment and true margin."

blocks.title: Set the trial period now
blocks.text: Decide the review date before you start. Six to twelve weeks is often long enough to see whether a shop reorders, while short enough that a weak channel does not drain you for a year.

takeaways: Score readiness on product consistency, paperwork, capacity, pricing headroom and cash.
Add a channel's monthly demand to your current sales and compare with your real maximum output.
Credit terms mean you fund stock before you are paid: calculate that cash.
Start with the channel that fits your product well and costs least to enter.

activity.title: Complete your readiness scorecard
steps: Score yourself 0, 1 or 2 on each of the five readiness areas and add up the total.
Write your current monthly output and your realistic maximum.
Pick one target channel and estimate its monthly demand and the cash it would tie up.
Place three possible channels on the fit and effort matrix.
Write your one-line channel decision with a review date.
activity.evidence: Your scored readiness sheet, capacity and cash calculation, and one-line channel decision.

lessons.title: Brand standards, price rules and written partner agreements
objectives: Write a one-page brand standards sheet that partners must keep to
Set a recommended retail price and a floor price you will not go below
List the terms every distribution agreement should cover
Decide your walk-away point before a partner negotiation

blocks.text: When other people sell your product, they carry your reputation. A customer who buys a jar from a pharmacy does not know or care that the pharmacist stored it beside a hot window; she only knows the butter was runny. Your protection is to decide, in writing, what must never change, and to agree it clearly with every partner.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: Two people with a signed agreement
blocks.caption: A short written agreement prevents most of the misunderstandings that end distribution relationships.

blocks.text: Your brand standards sheet
A **brand standards sheet** is one page that answers: what does a customer get, every time, wherever she buys? Keep it practical, not a slogan.

items: **Product:** the recipe or method, net weight or volume, and the quality checks each batch must pass.
**Packaging:** the exact container, lid, label design and colours; no handwritten or photocopied labels.
**Price:** your recommended retail price (RRP) for each size and your trade price for each type of partner.
**Presentation:** approved product photos and a short, honest description partners may use. No health or medical claims you cannot support.
**Storage and handling:** for example, keep below 30 °C and out of direct sunlight, if that is what your product needs.
**Customer care:** who handles complaints and how quickly.

blocks.text: Price rules: RRP, floor price and parity

Set a **recommended retail price** so a customer sees roughly the same price wherever she shops. Then set your **floor price**, the lowest trade price you will accept for each pack size. Work it out from your costs, not from a buyer's pressure: if a jar costs you 1,900 naira and you need at least 25% margin on what you receive, the floor is 1,900 / 0.75 = about 2,533 naira. Any deal below that loses you the profit you need.

Keep **price parity**: do not sell direct on Instagram far below the RRP your shops are charging. If a pharmacy sells at 4,000 naira and you sell at 3,200 online, the pharmacy loses customers to you and soon stops reordering. Run direct promotions carefully and tell partners in advance.
What every agreement should cover

blocks.title: Agreement terms checklist
items: Products, sizes and trade prices
Order minimum and delivery
Payment terms and method
Outright or consignment stock
Returns, damage and expiry
Review date and ending
blocks.caption: If a term is not written down, each side remembers it differently, so cover all six before the first delivery.

blocks.text: **Outright purchase** means the shop buys the stock and owns it; unsold units are its problem unless you agree otherwise. **Consignment** means you still own the stock on the shelf, and the shop pays only for what it sells after each count. Consignment is easier to get into a shop but riskier for you: write down who pays for damaged or missing units, how often you count, and how quickly payment follows the count.

Also cover **exclusivity and territory** if a partner asks for them. A distributor may want to be your only supplier in Kano, for example. Agree to exclusivity only for a limited period, a defined area and with a minimum order level, so you are not locked into a partner who stops buying.

blocks.title: Worked example: a one-page supply agreement
blocks.context: For example, Amaka agrees terms with a pharmacy owner in Garki for her 250 g shea butter.
steps: Product and price: 250 g jar at a trade price of 2,800 naira; RRP 4,000 naira, so the pharmacy keeps 1,200 naira, a 30% margin on the shelf price.
Order: minimum 12 jars, delivered within 3 working days of a WhatsApp order.
Payment: outright purchase, paid by bank transfer to her business account within 14 days of delivery.
Returns: jars damaged in delivery replaced at her cost if reported within 48 hours; no returns for jars kept in heat or past their best-before date.
Review: both sides review sales and terms after 8 weeks; either side may end with 2 weeks' written notice by WhatsApp or email.
blocks.result: Both signed a one-page sheet and each kept a photo. When a jar arrived cracked, the 48-hour rule settled it in one message instead of an argument.

blocks.title: Simple, but still serious
blocks.text: A one-page agreement signed by both sides is far better than a verbal deal. For larger contracts, exclusivity, or anything involving big sums, have a lawyer review the document before you sign.
Know your walk-away point

Before any negotiation, write your **walk-away point**: the deal you would rather refuse than accept. Negotiators call your best alternative if talks fail your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement). If your alternative is selling those same 96 jars to your own customers at full price, a buyer demanding a 50% discount and 90-day credit has a weak offer, and you can say no politely.

Pressure usually comes in three forms: a deeper discount for a bigger order, longer credit, or a cheaper ingredient to hit a lower price. Answer each from your sheet. A bigger order can earn a small volume discount only if your floor price still holds. Longer credit needs a price that covers the cost of waiting. A cheaper recipe changes the product your customers trust, so it stays off the table.

takeaways: Write one page of brand standards covering product, packaging, price, presentation, storage and care.
Set an RRP, a floor trade price calculated from cost, and keep price parity across channels.
Every agreement covers prices, orders, payment, stock ownership, returns and a review date.
Decide your walk-away point before you negotiate, not during.

activity.title: Draft your standards and terms
steps: Write your brand standards sheet using the six headings in this lesson.
Calculate the floor trade price for your main product from your unit cost and minimum margin.
Draft a one-page supply agreement for your chosen first channel using the six-term checklist.
Write your walk-away point for that negotiation in one sentence.
activity.evidence: Your brand standards sheet, floor price calculation and draft one-page agreement.

quiz.q: Amaka sells 260 jars at 4,000 naira on WhatsApp, 100 jars at 4,000 at a stall and 40 jars at 2,800 to a salon. What share of revenue comes from the salon?
quiz.explain: Salon revenue is 112,000 of a total 1,552,000 naira, which is 7.2%. 10% is its share of units, not revenue.

quiz.q: A chain wants 192 extra jars a month. A maker sells 400 a month now and can make at most 500. What is the best first response?
options: Start with a smaller number of branches that fits within her capacity
Accept the full order and work longer nights
Reduce supply to her loyal direct customers
quiz.explain: 592 jars exceeds her 500 maximum. Starting with fewer branches keeps quality and existing customers safe while proving the channel.

options: The shop owns the stock and pays on delivery
A distributor buys stock for many shops
An agent earns commission on each sale
The maker owns the stock on the shelf and is paid only for units that sell
quiz.explain: In consignment, ownership stays with you until a unit sells, so you need clear rules on counts, damage and payment timing.

quiz.q: A jar costs 1,900 naira to make and you need at least 25% margin on what you receive. What is your floor trade price?
quiz.explain: Floor = cost / (1 - 0.25) = 1,900 / 0.75 = about 2,533 naira. Adding 25% to cost (2,375) gives a 20% margin, not 25%.

quiz.q: A pharmacy sells your jar at the 4,000 naira RRP. You plan a 3,200 naira Instagram price for the whole month. What is the main risk?
options: The pharmacy loses customers to you and stops reordering
quiz.explain: Undercutting a partner's shelf price breaks price parity and damages the relationship.

quiz.q: Which product is least suited to a nationwide online marketplace as a first channel?
options: Heavy, fragile glass jars of body butter
quiz.explain: Heavy, fragile items are costly and risky to ship by courier, so a marketplace would be a small test at most.

modules.title: Channel Operations, Quality and True Margin
modules.overview: Each channel has its own order-to-cash process, and this module turns those processes into simple written routines. You then protect quality across every shelf with batch codes, stock rotation and a complaint trail, and finish by calculating the true profit each channel leaves you.

lessons.title: Order-to-cash routines for wholesale, consignment, marketplace and agent channels
objectives: Map the order-to-cash steps for each channel you use
Write a short standard operating procedure (SOP) for one channel
Calculate how long your cash is tied up under credit terms
Set up an order and payment log that shows who owes you what

blocks.text: Direct selling is simple: a customer orders, pays and receives. Distribution adds steps, people and waiting. **Order-to-cash** is the full path from the moment a partner orders to the moment the money is safely in your business account. When any step is unclear, orders go missing, deliveries are disputed and invoices are forgotten. A short written routine for each channel prevents most of this.

blocks.name: logistics
blocks.alt: Boxes being prepared and moved for delivery
blocks.caption: Every channel needs a clear route from order to delivery to payment.

blocks.title: Order-to-cash for a shop
items: Order received and confirmed
Pick, pack and invoice
Deliver and get signature
Follow up payment
Record and plan restock
blocks.caption: The sale is only finished when the money is recorded, not when the van leaves.

blocks.text: How the routine differs by channel

head: Channel
Key steps
Where it usually goes wrong
rows: Outright retail
Order, confirm, invoice, deliver with delivery note, collect payment on agreed date
No signed delivery note, so quantities are disputed later
Consignment
Deliver with a stock sheet, count on agreed dates, invoice for units sold, collect, top up
Counts skipped; damaged or missing units nobody agreed to pay for
Distributor
Bulk order, larger delivery, longer credit, regular statement of account
Long credit stretches your cash; one large unpaid invoice hurts badly
Online marketplace
List product, accept order, pack to platform rules, hand to courier or drop-off point, wait for payout
Late dispatch, poor packing, cancelled orders and returns
Agents
Issue stock or take orders, agent sells, agent pays in, you pay commission
Cash held by agents; stock with no record of who has what

blocks.text: Writing a short SOP

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a numbered list anyone on your team can follow without asking you. Keep it to one page per channel, written in the words your helpers use. Here is an example for outright retail orders.

items: When a shop orders on WhatsApp, reply within 2 hours confirming items, quantities, price and delivery day.
Enter the order in the order log with an order number, for example GK-014.
Pick jars from the oldest batch first, check each label and seal, and pack in a carton with padding.
Prepare two copies of the delivery note and one invoice showing order number, quantities, prices, total and payment due date.
At delivery, count together with the shop staff; both sign both delivery notes; leave one, bring one back.
Photograph the signed note and save it in the shop's WhatsApp chat and in your records folder.
One day before the due date, send a polite reminder with the invoice attached; record the payment the day it arrives.

blocks.text: Credit terms and your cash cycle

**Net 30** means the partner pays 30 days after the invoice date. It sounds harmless, but you paid for ingredients and jars well before you delivered. Count the days from when cash leaves your hands to when it comes back. This is your **cash cycle**.

blocks.title: Worked example: how long is the cash tied up?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka buys shea butter, oils and jars on 10 September for a 48-jar order from a distributor in Kaduna. Her cost is about 1,900 naira (approximate) per jar. The distributor pays net 30 from delivery.
steps: Cash out on 10 September: 48 x 1,900 = 91,200 naira for materials and labour.
She makes, cures and labels the jars, and delivers on 25 September (15 days later).
Payment is due 30 days after delivery: 25 October.
Cash cycle: 15 days of production + 30 days of credit = 45 days.
If the distributor pays 10 days late, the cycle becomes 55 days.
blocks.result: Amaka needs 91,200 naira of her own money locked away for about six to eight weeks per order. Before agreeing to a second distributor, she checks that she has enough working cash for both cycles at once.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Take partner payments only into your business account, never into a helper's or agent's personal account. Confirm every transfer in your banking app before releasing stock, because fake transfer alerts and screenshots are a common fraud. Never share your banking PIN or one-time passwords with anyone.
Your order and payment log

A simple Google Sheet with one row per order is enough. Use these columns: order number, date, partner, channel, product and quantity, invoice value, due date, date paid, amount paid, balance and notes. Add a filter so you can see everything unpaid, sorted by due date. Each Monday, look at the unpaid list and send reminders. A business that is owed a lot of money by partners can be profitable on paper and still unable to buy materials.

For marketplaces, also record the payout you actually received for each order, since fees and returns mean it is often less than the listed price. For agents, record stock issued to each agent, units sold, cash paid in and commission paid out, so that at any moment you know who holds your stock and your money.

blocks.title: Review channels on a fixed date
blocks.text: Put a review in your calendar three months after opening each new channel. Look at orders, on-time payment and returns. A fixed date stops you from quitting too early in frustration or hanging on for a year out of hope.

takeaways: Order-to-cash ends when the money is recorded, not when goods leave.
Write a one-page SOP per channel that a helper can follow without you.
Credit terms create a cash cycle: count days from paying for materials to receiving payment.
Keep one order and payment log and check the unpaid list every week.

activity.title: Write one SOP and start your log
steps: Choose the channel you use most after direct sales, or the one you plan to open.
Write its order-to-cash SOP in 5 to 8 numbered steps.
Create an order and payment log with the columns from this lesson and enter your last five orders.
Calculate the cash cycle in days for one recent or planned credit order.
activity.evidence: Your one-page SOP and a screenshot of your order and payment log with five entries.

lessons.title: Keeping quality consistent on every shelf: batch codes, stock rotation and complaints
objectives: Give every batch a code and trace where it went
Apply first-expired, first-out stock rotation with partners
Run a shelf check and act on what you find
Handle a quality complaint that arrives through a partner

blocks.text: At your stall, you can see if a jar looks wrong before a customer picks it up. In a shop forty kilometres away, you cannot. Quality across channels depends on three habits: knowing which batch went where, making sure old stock sells before new stock, and treating every complaint as information to trace and fix.

blocks.name: package
blocks.caption: Each carton you dispatch should be traceable to the batch it came from.

blocks.text: Batch codes and a batch record

A **batch code** is a short label that identifies when and how a group of products was made. A simple format is product, date and batch number for that day: for example **SB-2409-02** means shea butter, made in September 2024 (24-09), second batch of the day. Print or stamp it on every jar alongside the best-before date.

Keep a **batch record** for each code: date, ingredients used and their supplier lot numbers if available, quantity made, who made it, quality checks done, and where every unit went. If your product is NAFDAC-registered, the product you supply must match what was registered; speak to NAFDAC before changing your formula, pack size or label, and keep your batch records ready to show.

blocks.title: The quality loop across channels
items: Make and code batch
Record where it went
Check shelves
Log feedback
Fix the cause
blocks.caption: Each turn of the loop catches problems earlier, so fewer reach customers.

blocks.text: Stock rotation with partners

Use **FEFO: first expired, first out**. When you restock a shelf, move older jars to the front and put new ones behind. Shop staff often do the opposite because new cartons are easier to place at the front. Agree in writing that whoever restocks rotates the stock, and do it yourself during visits.

items: Check best-before dates on every shelf visit. Agree in advance what happens to stock within, for example, two months of its date: a promotion, a swap or collection.
Ask partners to store your product as your label says: for example away from direct sun, generators and hot shop windows.
Do not overstock. A shelf holding six months of sales ages your stock and ties up your money. Supply in smaller, more frequent drops.

blocks.text: The shelf check

Visit or ask for photos every two to four weeks. Use the same short checklist each time: Is the product on the shelf and visible? Is the price label correct and close to the RRP? Are any jars damaged, dusty or past date? Is stock rotated? How many units are left? Note the answers in your log. Remaining units also tell you **sell-through**, which you will use to decide whether to grow this channel.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a complaint
blocks.context: For example, a pharmacy in Garki tells Amaka that a customer returned a jar of shea butter that had separated and felt oily. The jar's code is SB-2409-02.
steps: She thanks the pharmacy, offers the customer a replacement through the shop, and asks for a photo of the jar and where it was kept.
Her batch record shows SB-2409-02 made 60 jars: 24 to the Garki pharmacy, 24 to a Wuse salon and 12 sold direct.
She checks the shelf photo: the pharmacy displays jars in a window that gets afternoon sun.
She asks the salon and her direct buyers about that batch. No problems reported; the salon stores jars inside a cabinet.
Cause: heat exposure at one outlet, not the batch. She swaps the 9 jars remaining in Garki and agrees a new shelf away from the window.
blocks.result: One complaint, handled in two days, ended with a better shelf position and no wider recall. Without the batch code, she could not have shown that the other 36 jars were fine.

blocks.title: When it could be unsafe
blocks.text: If a complaint suggests a safety risk (a skin reaction, contamination, mould, a foreign object in food), stop supplying that batch, collect remaining units from all outlets that received it, and tell the customer to stop using it. For a regulated product, report it to NAFDAC. Speed matters more than embarrassment.
Returns and damaged stock

Agree a clear returns rule with each partner (see your agreement from Module 1). Typical points: damage on arrival reported within a short window is replaced by you; damage from poor storage at the shop is not; expired stock is handled as agreed. Record every return with the batch code and reason. Over a few months the returns log shows patterns, for example lids cracking in transit, which point to a fix in packaging rather than a dispute with a partner.

Finally, close the loop with your team. If the same question or complaint arrives twice from different outlets, put it on the agenda for your next production meeting. Quality problems found in distribution are often solved in the kitchen or the packing area.

takeaways: Code every batch and record where each unit went.
Rotate stock first expired, first out, and supply little and often.
Run the same shelf check every two to four weeks and record sell-through.
Trace complaints by batch before deciding the cause; act fast on any safety risk.

activity.title: Set up traceability
steps: Design your batch code format and write three example codes.
Create a batch record template with the columns from this lesson.
Write a five-question shelf checklist.
Carry out one shelf check (or a check of your own stock) and record the results.
activity.evidence: Your batch record template with at least one completed batch, and one completed shelf checklist.

lessons.title: Channel economics: the margin waterfall and true profit per channel
objectives: Work out your trade price backwards from the shelf price and each partner's margin
Tell margin and markup apart when a partner quotes a percentage
Calculate the true profit per unit for each channel after fees and costs
Use profit per channel and capacity to decide where to grow

blocks.text: A channel can bring impressive sales and still lose you money. To know which channels build your business, calculate what each one actually leaves you after the partner's share, fees, delivery and your production cost. Start from the shelf price and walk backwards. This is often called a **margin waterfall**.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Calculate each channel's true profit instead of assuming it.

blocks.text: Margin versus markup

Partners usually talk in **margin**: the share of their selling price they keep. Many small producers think in **markup**: what they add on top of cost. They are not the same. If a shop buys at 2,800 naira and sells at 4,000, it keeps 1,200 naira. As a margin that is 1,200 / 4,000 = 30%. As a markup it is 1,200 / 2,800 = 42.9%. When a shop says "we need 30%", ask: 30% of the shelf price, or 30% added to your trade price? The difference is real money.
Walking back from the shelf price

blocks.title: Margin waterfall for one jar
items: Shelf price 4,000 naira
Retailer keeps 1,200
Distributor keeps 280
You receive 2,520
Cost 1,900, profit 620
blocks.caption: When a distributor sits between you and the shop, both margins come out of the same 4,000 naira shelf price.

blocks.text: The retailer keeps 30% of 4,000 = 1,200, so it pays 2,800. A distributor that keeps 10% of its selling price to the shop keeps 280 of that 2,800 and pays you 2,520. Your cost of 1,900 leaves you 620 naira per jar. Selling the same jar direct for 4,000 would leave far more, but the distributor may sell hundreds of jars you could never reach yourself.
Fees and costs that hide in each channel

items: **Payment processing:** Paystack's published fee for local Nigerian transactions is 1.5% plus 100 naira, with the 100 naira waived under 2,500 naira and the total capped at 2,000 naira per transaction. Check the current rate before you calculate, since providers change prices.
**Marketplace fees:** commission and any fulfilment or listing fees vary by platform and category. Read the current rate in the seller centre; never guess.
**Delivery to partners:** the transport cost of a delivery divided by the units delivered.
**Agent commission:** a fixed amount or percentage per unit sold.
**Marketing:** for direct sales, divide what you spend on ads in a month by the orders they bring.

blocks.title: Worked example: true profit per jar by channel
blocks.context: For example, Amaka's 250 g jar costs about 1,900 naira (approximate) to make. RRP is 4,000 naira. The marketplace commission below is a 10% assumption for practice only; she will replace it with the real rate for her category.
steps: Direct with a Paystack link: fee 1.5% of 4,000 = 60 + 100 = 160; ads 30,000 naira a month / 100 orders = 300 per jar. Profit: 4,000 - 160 - 300 - 1,900 = 1,640 naira.
Pharmacy, outright: receives 2,800; delivery 2,400 naira per trip / 24 jars = 100. Profit: 2,800 - 100 - 1,900 = 800 naira.
Distributor: receives 2,520; distributor collects from her. Profit: 2,520 - 1,900 = 620 naira.
Marketplace (assumed 10%): commission 400; shipping packaging 150. Profit: 4,000 - 400 - 150 - 1,900 = 1,550 naira.
Agent at 10% commission: commission 400; delivery to agent 50. Profit: 4,000 - 400 - 50 - 1,900 = 1,650 naira.
blocks.result: Per jar, direct and agent sales leave the most profit, and the distributor the least. But profit per jar is only half the picture: the distributor might move 300 jars a month (186,000 naira profit) with no ads and no chatting, while direct sales may be stuck at 100 orders (164,000 naira).

head: Channel
You receive per jar (naira)
Profit per jar (naira)
Profit as % of what you receive
rows: Direct
Pharmacy
Distributor
Marketplace (assumed fee)
Agent

blocks.text: Capacity changes the answer

If your kitchen can make only 500 jars a month, every jar should go where it earns most, as long as demand exists. If you can make far more than you sell, a low-margin channel that moves large volumes adds profit you would not otherwise earn. So compare channels on **total monthly profit** and on **your time**, not just on profit per unit. A channel that needs ten hours of chatting for 30 sales may be worse than a distributor order that takes two hours.

blocks.title: Do not forget waiting costs
blocks.text: A channel that pays in 45 days ties up your cash. If you have to borrow to fund that stock, the interest is a real cost of the channel. Include it, or ask for shorter terms for a slightly lower price.
Repeat this calculation every quarter with real figures from your order log. Prices, fees and delivery costs change, and a channel that was healthy last year can quietly turn thin.

takeaways: Walk back from the shelf price: each partner's margin comes out of it before you are paid.
Margin is a share of the selling price; markup is added to cost. Always ask which one is meant.
True profit per channel subtracts fees, delivery, commission, marketing and your unit cost.
Decide on total monthly profit, time and capacity, not on profit per unit alone.

activity.title: Build your channel profit table
steps: Write your unit cost and RRP for your main product.
For each channel you use or plan, list every deduction: partner margin, fees, delivery, commission, marketing.
Calculate profit per unit and profit as a percentage of what you receive.
Multiply by realistic monthly volume to get monthly profit per channel.
Circle the channel that gives the best total profit for the time and capacity it uses.
activity.evidence: A channel profit table (Google Sheet or paper photo) with every deduction shown and monthly totals.

quiz.q: A shop buys at 2,800 naira and sells at 4,000. What is its margin on the selling price?
quiz.explain: Margin = 1,200 / 4,000 = 30%. 42.9% is the markup on the 2,800 cost.

quiz.q: Materials are bought on 1 March, goods delivered on 16 March, and the partner pays net 30 from delivery. What is the cash cycle?
quiz.explain: 15 days from paying for materials to delivery, plus 30 days of credit, is 45 days.

quiz.q: A customer complains about a jar with code SB-2409-02. What should the maker do first?
options: Recall every product she has ever made
Ignore it because only one customer complained
Check the batch record to see where that batch went and ask other outlets about it
quiz.explain: The batch record shows where the batch went, so she can tell whether the problem is the batch or one outlet's storage.

quiz.q: A shelf check shows new jars at the front and older jars hidden behind. What is the right action?
options: Move older jars to the front so they sell first (FEFO)
Collect all old jars and throw them away
Reduce the price of the new jars
quiz.explain: First expired, first out means older stock goes to the front so it sells before its date.

quiz.q: With Paystack's published local fee (1.5% + 100 naira), what is the fee on a 4,000 naira payment?
quiz.explain: 1.5% of 4,000 is 60, plus the 100 naira flat fee (not waived because 4,000 is above 2,500) gives 160 naira.

quiz.q: A distributor gives 620 naira profit per jar on 300 jars a month; direct sales give 1,640 naira on 100 jars. Which statement is correct?
options: The distributor earns more total monthly profit (186,000 vs 164,000 naira)
Direct sales always earn more in total
quiz.explain: 300 x 620 = 186,000 and 100 x 1,640 = 164,000, so the distributor brings more total profit despite the lower per-jar figure.

modules.title: Winning Partners, Building an Agent Network and Planning Growth
modules.overview: You learn to pitch retailers with a sell sheet and a trial offer, judge results with sell-through, and build partnerships beyond simple wholesale. You then recruit, train and manage agents safely, and finish by assembling your distribution portfolio and a 90-day plan for one new channel.

lessons.title: Pitching retailers, trial orders and partnerships beyond wholesale
objectives: Prepare a one-page sell sheet and a sample pack for retail buyers
Run a pitch that ends with a small, low-risk trial order
Measure a trial with sell-through and reorder timing
Identify partnership routes such as bundles, gifting and trade fairs

blocks.text: A shop owner's real question is not "is this product nice?" but "will it sell from my shelf and make me money without trouble?" Your pitch must answer that question with facts: who buys it, what the shop earns per unit, how reliably you deliver and what you do if something goes wrong.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.caption: A good pitch is a short business conversation backed by a one-page sell sheet.

blocks.text: Your sell sheet
A **sell sheet** is one page, printed and as a PDF for WhatsApp, that a buyer can keep. Include:

items: Product photo, name, sizes and the problem it solves for the customer, in one or two lines.
RRP, trade price and the shop's margin per unit in naira and as a percentage.
Minimum order, delivery area and lead time, payment terms.
Registration details where they apply (CAC number, NAFDAC number), batch coding and best-before.
Proof that it sells: approximate monthly sales, repeat customers, any outlets that already stock you (with their permission).
Your contact details and business account name.

blocks.text: The pitch pipeline

blocks.title: From target list to regular orders
items: List target outlets
Visit and observe shelves
Pitch with samples
Small trial order
Review and reorder
blocks.caption: Move each outlet one stage at a time and record where every one stands.

items: List 10 to 15 outlets whose customers match yours: pharmacies, salons, gyms, mini-marts, gift shops.
Visit first as a shopper. Note similar products, their prices, where they sit and who decides what is stocked.
Ask for a short meeting with the decision maker, ideally at a quiet hour, not on a busy Saturday.
In the meeting: one sentence on the customer, show and let them try the sample, give the margin per unit, then offer a small trial.
Agree the trial in writing: quantity, price, terms and review date. Follow up the same day with the sell sheet and agreement.

blocks.text: A **trial order** lowers the buyer's risk: for example 12 units, with an agreement to review after 4 to 6 weeks. Some shops will ask for consignment for the first order. That can be reasonable for a trial, as long as the count dates and payment terms are written down.

Follow up without pestering. If a buyer says "come back next month", write the date in your pipeline and return on that date with something new: a stockist update, a customer review, or a fresh sample. Record every outlet's stage (target, visited, met, trial, regular) so you always know where your next order is most likely to come from. A "no" today is often a "not yet"; keep the door open politely.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a trial
blocks.context: For example, Amaka lists 12 target outlets in Abuja, gets 5 meetings and 2 trial orders of 12 jars each, at a pharmacy and a gym.
steps: Conversion: 2 trials from 12 targets is about 17%; from 5 meetings it is 40%.
After 4 weeks the pharmacy has sold 9 of 12 jars: sell-through 9 / 12 = 75%.
The gym has sold 3 of 12 jars: sell-through 3 / 12 = 25%.
The pharmacy reorders 24 jars on day 30. The gym makes no reorder and the jars sit behind the counter.
She asks the gym why. Members did not see the jars, and the staff could not answer questions about the product.
blocks.result: The pharmacy becomes a regular account. For the gym she offers a small shelf sign and a 15-minute staff briefing, with a second review in 4 weeks; if sell-through stays low she collects the stock and moves on.

blocks.title: Use each win to earn the next
blocks.text: With the partner's permission, mention current stockists in your next pitch and post where customers can buy you on your social media. Your direct channels can send buyers into shops, which helps those shops reorder.
Partnerships beyond wholesale

items: **Bundles and co-branding:** a body butter and a handmade soap from another maker sold together as a gift set, with costs and profits split in writing.
**Corporate and event gifting:** companies, hotels and event planners buying in bulk for staff gifts, guests or souvenirs, often with a custom label sleeve.

**Trade fairs and exhibitions:** events run by chambers of commerce, trade associations and women's business networks put you in front of many retail buyers in one day. Bring samples, sell sheets and a sign-up sheet for follow-up.
**Organisations that serve your customers:** cooperatives, associations or community groups that can introduce your product to their members.

blocks.text: Every partnership must still fit your brand standards and floor price. A gift set that requires you to cut quality or sell below your floor is a bad deal however famous the partner.

blocks.title: Avoid channel conflict
blocks.text: When you add partners in the same area, tell existing partners, keep price parity, and do not quietly offer a new shop better terms than a loyal one. Partners who discover that will feel cheated.

takeaways: Pitch with a one-page sell sheet that shows the buyer's margin, terms and proof of sales.
Ask for a small trial order with a written review date.
Judge trials by sell-through and whether the outlet reorders, then support or exit.
Bundles, gifting, trade fairs and partner organisations can open routes a shop pitch cannot.

activity.title: Prepare your pitch kit
steps: Create a one-page sell sheet in Canva or Google Docs using the six items above.
Write a target list of 10 outlets with the name of the decision maker where you know it.
Visit two outlets as a shopper and record competing products and prices.
Write a 60-second pitch script that ends with a trial offer.
activity.evidence: Your sell sheet PDF, target list with stages, and pitch script.

lessons.title: Recruiting, training and managing agents and partner staff
objectives: Choose between a commission model and a reseller-discount model for agents
Prepare an agent starter kit and run a short training session
Set stock, cash and safety rules for agents
Track agent performance with a monthly scorecard

blocks.text: Agents and resellers can carry your product into estates, offices, churches, mosques and markets you never visit. They also carry your reputation. An agent who promises results your product cannot deliver, or who keeps customers' money, damages trust you spent years building. This lesson is about building an agent network that stays honest and productive.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A person teaching a small group
blocks.caption: Agents sell better and more honestly when you train them properly.

blocks.text: Two ways to pay agents

head: Model
How it works
Best when
rows: Commission
Agent takes orders and sends them to you or collects payment into your account; you deliver and pay the agent a fixed amount or percentage per sale
You want control of stock, cash and customer details
Reseller discount
Agent buys stock from you at a discount and resells at RRP, keeping the difference
Agents have their own capital and you want them to carry stock risk

blocks.text: Recruiting the right agents

Look for people who already talk to your kind of customer every day: a hairdresser, a pharmacy attendant, a fitness coach, a women's group leader, a busy office administrator. Ask for a referee who has known them for some time, take a copy of a valid ID, and record their phone number and home area. Start with three to five agents you can train and support well, rather than twenty you cannot follow up. A small, active network beats a long list of names who never sell.

Be honest in your recruiting message. Say what a realistic month looks like, for example "most agents sell 10 to 30 jars a month" only if your own records show that. Never promise income you cannot back with numbers, and never charge agents a registration fee to join; schemes that make money from recruiting people rather than selling products are a warning sign of a pyramid scheme.

Keep the terms the **same for every agent at the same level**. Negotiating differently with each person creates resentment when agents compare notes, which they will. You may reward high performers with a higher tier, but publish the rule: for example, 10% commission, rising to 12% for agents who sell more than 50 units a month.
The agent starter kit

items: Price list with RRP for each product and the agent's commission or discount.
A product facts sheet: ingredients, sizes, how to use, storage, and the claims agents may and may not make.
Approved photos and short captions for WhatsApp Status, plus the link to your WhatsApp Business catalog.
Answers to the ten questions customers ask most.
The order process, payment details for your business account, and a contact for complaints.

blocks.text: A 60-minute training session

items: 10 minutes: the brand story and who the product is for.
15 minutes: hands-on with the product; each agent tries it and practises explaining it in their own words.
10 minutes: prices, commission and how orders and payments flow.
15 minutes: role play of common customer questions and one complaint.
10 minutes: stock, cash and safety rules; each agent signs the agent agreement.

blocks.title: Stock, cash and data rules
blocks.text: Customers pay into your business account or a payment link in your business name, never into an agent's personal account. Limit stock held by any new agent to a small amount until trust is built, and record every unit issued. Keep customer phone numbers and addresses private: agents must not add customers to groups or share their details without permission.

blocks.title: The agent management cycle
items: Recruit carefully
Train and equip
Track monthly
Review and reward
Refresh or release
blocks.caption: Run the cycle every month so strong agents grow and inactive ones are noticed early.

blocks.title: Worked example: monthly agent scorecard
blocks.context: For example, Amaka recruits 5 agents in Abuja on a 10% commission on the 4,000 naira RRP, which is 400 naira per jar.
steps: Units sold in October: Ifeoma 40, Hauwa 25, Bisi 12, Ngozi 8, Ruth 0.
Total units: 40 + 25 + 12 + 8 + 0 = 85 jars; revenue 85 x 4,000 = 340,000 naira.
Commission: 85 x 400 = 34,000 naira in total; Ifeoma earns 40 x 400 = 16,000 naira.
Ifeoma and Hauwa together sold 65 of 85 jars, about 76% of agent sales.
Ruth has sold nothing for two months; Bisi and Ngozi had several customers ask about a smaller size.
blocks.result: Amaka asks Ifeoma to share her approach at the next agent call, offers Ruth a refresher or a friendly exit, and passes the smaller-size request to her production plan as a product idea to test.

blocks.text: Partner staff count too

In shops, the staff who stand near the shelf decide whether customers hear about you. Leave a simple product card, brief staff in five minutes during restock visits, and tell them how to reach you with questions. Thank staff who report problems early.
Close the feedback loop

Set up a short monthly call or WhatsApp voice note with your agents. Ask three questions: What sold? What did customers ask that you could not answer? What complaints did you hear? Record the answers. When the same comment arrives from several agents or outlets, take it to your production and packaging decisions. Agents are often your best early warning system and your best source of new product ideas.

takeaways: Choose commission or reseller discount, and apply the same published terms to every agent.
Give each agent a starter kit and a one-hour training before they sell.
Payments go to your business account; stock and customer data are controlled and recorded.
Track agents monthly with a scorecard and use their feedback to improve products.

activity.title: Design your agent programme
steps: Choose commission or reseller discount and write the rates and tiers.
Assemble a starter kit: price list, facts sheet, photos, FAQs and order process.
Write your stock, cash and data rules in five lines.
Create a monthly scorecard template with units, revenue, commission and feedback columns.
activity.evidence: Your agent terms, starter kit files and scorecard template.

lessons.title: Your distribution portfolio and 90-day expansion plan
objectives: Assemble a distribution portfolio with channel revenue, true margin and proof
Complete a brand consistency check across every channel
Write a 90-day plan for one new channel with dated milestones
Set decision rules to expand, adjust or exit a channel at day 90

blocks.text: This lesson brings the course together into the capstone: a distribution portfolio that shows what works today, and a 90-day plan that opens one new channel properly. Buyers, distributors, lenders and grant programmes all respond better to a producer who can show real figures and a clear plan than to one with good intentions.

blocks.name: master-plan
blocks.alt: A person planning on a large board
blocks.caption: A dated plan turns your expansion idea into weekly actions.

blocks.text: Part 1: the channel breakdown

Take your baseline from Module 1 and your profit table from Module 2 and combine them for the last one to three months: each channel's units, revenue, share of revenue, true profit per unit, total profit and share of profit. Add one line on payment behaviour, such as "pays on time" or "average 12 days late".

head: Channel
Revenue share
Profit share
Note
rows: Direct (WhatsApp, Instagram)
High margin, depends on ads and her time
Stall
Saturday only, weather-dependent
Pharmacy (2 branches)
Lower margin, steady reorders, pays on time

blocks.text: The table above is for example only, but notice what it shows: the pharmacy brings 18% of revenue but only 8% of profit. That is acceptable if it is growing, brings new customers and takes little of her time. The portfolio is where you make those trade-offs visible.
Part 2: the brand consistency check
Visit or request photos from every outlet and check your own online listings. Score each item yes or no for every channel:

items: Same label, packaging and pack sizes everywhere; no old designs still on shelves.
Shelf or listing price within your RRP range; no partner undercut.
Product photos and descriptions match your brand standards sheet, with no unsupported claims.
Stock rotated and within date; stored as the label says.
Complaints answered within your stated time.

blocks.text: Part 3: the 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day channel plan
items: Days 1-15: fix readiness gaps
Days 16-30: build pitch kit
Days 31-60: pitch and trial
Days 61-90: review and decide
blocks.caption: Each phase has a clear output, so you can see in any week whether the plan is on track.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amaka's 90-day plan for pharmacies
blocks.context: For example, Amaka decides her next channel is independent pharmacies in Abuja, building on her first two branches.
steps: Days 1 to 15: add a production day to raise capacity from 500 to about 600 jars a month; print batch codes; set aside 200,000 naira working cash for credit terms.
Days 16 to 30: update her sell sheet with current stockists (with permission) and the 30% shop margin; list 15 target pharmacies; prepare 15 sample jars.
Days 31 to 60: aim for 8 meetings and 4 trial orders of 12 jars; deliver within 3 days; first shelf check after 2 weeks.
Days 61 to 90: measure each outlet's sell-through, payment timing and true profit; hold a review with each one.
Targets: at least 3 outlets reordering, sell-through of 60% or more within 6 weeks, payments within the agreed 14 days, and a true profit of at least 750 naira per jar.
blocks.result: By writing the targets before she starts, Amaka knows exactly what success means. If she hits them, she adds a further 4 pharmacies in the next 90 days; if not, she studies why before spending more.

blocks.text: Decision rules at day 90

items: **Expand** when most targets are met: add outlets at the same pace your capacity and cash allow.
**Adjust** when sales are there but margin or payments are weak: renegotiate terms, change pack size, or shorten credit.
**Exit** when sell-through stays low after support and the channel uses more time and cash than it returns. Collect your stock politely and keep the relationship friendly.

blocks.text: Common mistakes to avoid

items: **Targets without numbers.** "Grow in pharmacies" cannot be judged at day 90; "3 outlets reordering" can.
**No cash plan.** Credit channels need working cash set aside before the first delivery, not after.
**Skipping the shelf checks.** Problems found in week two are cheap to fix; problems found in week ten have already cost you customers.
**Changing the product mid-trial.** If you change the recipe, jar or price during the 90 days, you cannot tell what caused the result.
**Forgetting existing customers.** Keep your direct buyers served and informed; they are still your most profitable channel.

blocks.text: If you plan to approach a bigger partner later, such as a supermarket chain or a regional distributor, your portfolio becomes your strongest argument. Show three things: steady sell-through at your current outlets, reliable on-time delivery from your order log, and enough capacity and cash to meet a larger order. Ask early for the partner's written supplier requirements, so your next 90-day plan can close those gaps one by one.

blocks.title: Keep the plan small
blocks.text: One new channel per 90 days, done well, usually beats three opened at once. Each new channel needs your attention during its first weeks, when most problems appear.

Present your portfolio and plan in a short document or a few slides with your brand colours. Keep supporting evidence in a folder: signed agreements, delivery notes, the order log, shelf-check photos and agent scorecards. This is the shift the course has worked towards: from selling a product yourself to running a brand that others help to sell, with the numbers to prove it is working.

takeaways: Show each channel's revenue share and profit share side by side.
Check brand consistency at every outlet and listing, not just your own shelf.
Plan 90 days in four phases with written targets set before you start.
At day 90, decide to expand, adjust or exit using your targets.

activity.title: Draft your capstone
steps: Build your channel breakdown table with revenue share, profit share and a note for each channel.
Complete the brand consistency check for every channel you use.
Write your 90-day plan in four phases with dated tasks.
Write four measurable targets and your expand, adjust or exit rules.
activity.evidence: Your channel breakdown, completed consistency checklist and dated 90-day plan.

quiz.q: A pharmacy sold 9 of the 12 jars delivered in 4 weeks. What is its sell-through?
A gym's trial shows 25% sell-through and no reorder. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Ask why, offer simple support such as a shelf sign and staff briefing, then review again
Send a bigger order to push sales
Cut the price below your floor
quiz.explain: Find the cause first. Visibility and staff knowledge are common, fixable reasons; if it stays low after support, exit politely.

quiz.q: Five agents sold 85 jars at a 400 naira commission each. What is the total commission?
quiz.explain: 85 x 400 = 34,000 naira. 340,000 naira is the revenue.

quiz.q: Which rule best protects money in an agent network?
options: Agents collect cash and pay you monthly
Customers pay into your business account or a link in your business name
Each agent negotiates their own commission
New agents hold large stock to sell faster
quiz.explain: Payments into your business account keep cash under your control and reduce fraud risk.

quiz.q: A channel brings 18% of revenue but 8% of profit. What does this tell you?
options: It must be closed at once
It has a lower margin than your other channels, so judge it on growth, time used and new customers too
It is your most profitable channel
quiz.explain: Profit share below revenue share means a lower margin. It may still be worth keeping if it grows and costs little time.

quiz.q: Which is the best target for day 90 of a channel plan?
options: At least 3 outlets reordering with 60% sell-through in 6 weeks
quiz.explain: A target with numbers and a time frame lets you decide clearly whether to expand, adjust or exit.

finalQuiz.q: Which channel usually pays you only for units that have sold, after a stock count?
finalQuiz.explain: In consignment you own the stock on the shelf and are paid for sold units after each count.

finalQuiz.q: A maker sells 400 units a month, can make 500, and a new partner wants 150 a month. What is the gap?
finalQuiz.explain: 400 + 150 = 550, which is 50 more than the 500 maximum.

finalQuiz.q: Stock costing 1,500 naira a unit, 100 units, is delivered on net 30 credit. How much of the maker's cash is tied up until payment, before profit?
finalQuiz.explain: 100 x 1,500 = 150,000 naira of cost is funded by the maker until the partner pays.

options: Charging every partner the same trade price
Keeping the customer's price broadly the same across channels so you do not undercut partners
finalQuiz.explain: Parity means a customer sees roughly the same price wherever she buys, which protects partner relationships.

finalQuiz.q: A buyer pushes for a price below your floor in exchange for a large order. What should guide your answer?
options: Your floor price and walk-away point, decided before the meeting
The size of the order alone
What the buyer says competitors charge
finalQuiz.explain: Your floor comes from your costs and minimum margin. Prepare it, and your alternative, before negotiating.

finalQuiz.q: Which item is most important on a signed delivery note?
options: The quantities counted and signed by both sides
finalQuiz.explain: A signed count prevents disputes about how many units were delivered.

finalQuiz.q: A complaint arrives about one jar. The batch record shows the same batch went to three outlets with no other complaints, and the complaining outlet stores jars in a sunny window. What is the likely cause?
finalQuiz.explain: Tracing by batch shows the batch performed well elsewhere, which points to storage at one outlet.

finalQuiz.q: A shop buys at 3,000 naira and sells at 5,000. What is its margin?
finalQuiz.explain: Margin = 2,000 / 5,000 = 40%. 66.7% is the markup on the 3,000 cost.

finalQuiz.q: Shelf price 5,000; retailer keeps 30%; distributor keeps 10% of its selling price to the retailer. What does the maker receive?
finalQuiz.explain: Retailer pays 5,000 x 0.70 = 3,500. Distributor keeps 350 and pays 3,150.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a maker confirm every transfer in her banking app before releasing stock?
options: Because fake alerts and screenshots are a common fraud
finalQuiz.explain: Fake credit alerts and edited screenshots are common; only a confirmed credit in your account counts.

finalQuiz.q: An agent has sold nothing for two months. What is the best management step?
options: Offer a refresher session or a friendly exit, and record the decision
finalQuiz.explain: The monthly cycle spots inactive agents early: support them or release them cleanly.

finalQuiz.q: At day 90 a new channel meets sales targets but payments are always late. Which decision rule fits?
options: Adjust: renegotiate or shorten credit terms
finalQuiz.explain: Sales are working, so adjust the weak part (payment terms) before expanding further.

capstone.title: Distribution Expansion Plan
capstone.brief: Produce a distribution portfolio and plan: a channel-by-channel revenue and true-margin breakdown of your current sales, a brand consistency checklist covering packaging, pricing and quality across channels, and a 90-day plan to open one new channel with readiness requirements, outreach steps and measurable targets.
steps: Collect one to three months of sales records and build your channel baseline (Module 1, Lesson 1).
Calculate true profit per unit and per month for each channel, showing every deduction (Module 2, Lesson 3).
Combine both into a channel breakdown with revenue share, profit share and payment behaviour.
Complete the brand consistency check for every outlet, agent and listing.
Choose one new channel using your readiness score and the fit and effort matrix.
Write a four-phase 90-day plan with dated tasks, outreach list, sell sheet and draft agreement.
Set four measurable targets and your expand, adjust or exit rules for day 90.
evidence: Channel breakdown table with revenue share, profit per unit and profit share for every channel
Brand standards sheet and completed brand consistency checklist
Readiness scorecard with capacity and cash calculations
Sell sheet, target outlet list and draft one-page supply agreement
Dated 90-day plan with measurable targets and decision rules
